idiom_name: explicit return values; map vs forEach; promise chaining
implementation_notes: A JavaScript function that falls off its end returns undefined, so the discipline is about saying what a function produces: Array.prototype.map exists to produce a new array - MDN calls calling it without using the result an anti-pattern - while forEach always returns undefined and is deliberately not chainable, and a promise chain only stays a chain because every .then callback returns a value (a callback with no return hands the next step undefined). Where the caller is expected to continue on the same object, returning this is the library convention (jQuery, chai assertions), not a language rule. Nothing warns about an unused result, so the contract lives in naming, JSDoc/types and lint rules.
code_sketch:
const active = users.filter((u) => u.active);        // a value, not a mutation
const names  = active.map((u) => u.name);            // new array returned
users.forEach((u) => log.debug(u.id));               // undefined: side effects

const json = await fetch(url).then((r) => r.json()); // return keeps the chain
pitfalls: A callback that returns nothing inside map produces an array of undefined, and automatic semicolon insertion turns a return split across lines into a bare return.
A .then callback that does not return its value or promise starts a floating operation: the chain settles before the work finishes and rejections escape it.

mutating methods and producing methods are mixed in the same prototype - push returns a length, sort returns the same array, slice returns a new one - so aliasing bugs follow from assuming the wrong convention.
